The team's final model is Gerard's **C0**: the "portable" model, which carries from the developed market (Part 1) to
the emerging market (Part 2). It is a set of **Tweedie generalised linear models (GLMs)**, one or two per line. This
page shows how a single prediction is built, the maths behind each step, and lets you explore every rating factor
exactly as the [underwriting calculator](underwriting-calculator.qmd) uses it.

## 1. The idea in one line

A GLM starts from a **base cost** and multiplies it up or down by one **relativity** per rating factor:

$$
\text{expected cost} \;=\; \text{base} \times r_{\text{age}} \times r_{\text{flood zone}} \times r_{\text{excess}} \times \cdots \times \text{exposure}
$$

A relativity above 1 makes the policy dearer and below 1 cheaper. Because every factor has its own visible
multiplier, an actuary can explain any premium line by line. That's the main reason we chose GLMs over a black box
for the final model.

## 2. Model structure

| Line | Small claims | Large claims (above 50,000) | After the model |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Home contents** | Tweedie GLM, 17 factors + log sum insured | none: no split | level step ×0.866 |
| **Motor** | Tweedie GLM, 14 factors | Tweedie GLM, 3 factors, scaled to a Pareto tail | renewals ×0.861; new business ×1.05 |
| **Buildings** | XGBoost (trees, depth 3) | Tweedie GLM, scaled to a Pareto tail | ×0.957 |

*Buildings small claims use gradient-boosted trees, so they aren't in the calculator yet.*

How one motor prediction is put together:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  X["Policy<br/>rating factors"] --> S["Small-claim GLM<br/>exp(intercept + factors<br/>+ trend + log exposure)"]
  X --> L["Large-claim GLM<br/>exp(intercept + 3 factors<br/>+ trend + log exposure)"]
  L --> P["x Pareto adjustment"]
  S --> A["As-is cost<br/>small + large"]
  P --> A
  A --> V["Level step<br/>by segment"]
  V --> F["2025 prediction"]
```

## 3. The maths

### The distribution: Tweedie

Most policies have no claim in a year, and a few have a large one. The **Tweedie** distribution with power
$1 < p < 2$ handles both: it is a compound Poisson-gamma, with a point mass at zero and a continuous right tail. We use
$p = 1.5$, the same power the competition scores with:

$$
Y_i \sim \text{Tweedie}(\mu_i,\ \phi,\ p = 1.5), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i) = \phi\,\mu_i^{\,1.5}
$$

### The linear predictor, with log link and exposure offset

$$
\log \mu_i \;=\; \underbrace{\beta_0}_{\text{intercept}}
\;+\; \sum_{j} f_j(x_{ij})
\;+\; \underbrace{\gamma\,(2025 - \bar t)}_{\text{trend to 2025}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\log e_i}_{\text{offset}}
$$

The log link turns sums into products, which is why every factor becomes a multiplicative relativity $r_j = e^{f_j}$.
The offset fixes the coefficient on $\log e_i$ at 1, so cost is proportional to time on cover.

```{ojs}
md`For contents, the trend slope is γ = ${C.trend_slope.toFixed(4)} a year (+${((Math.exp(C.trend_slope) - 1) * 100).toFixed(1)}% a year), from a fitting-year
centre of t̄ = ${C.trend_origin.toFixed(2)}, so the 2025 trend multiplier is **×${C.trend_multiplier_2025.toFixed(4)}**. For motor it is
**×${Ms.trend_multiplier_2025.toFixed(4)}** (+${((Math.exp(Ms.trend_slope) - 1) * 100).toFixed(1)}% a year).`
```

### Four kinds of rating term

Each $f_j$ is one of these:

| Kind | $f_j(x)$ | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Categorical** | $\beta_{j,\ell(x)}$, with the base level $\beta_{j,\text{base}} = 0$ | cover type, flood zone, segment, age band |
| **Band** | $\beta_{j,k}$ for $c_{k-1} < x \le c_k$ | motor prior claims; NCB and years licensed in the large-claim GLM |
| **Spline** | $a_0 + a_1 d + a_2 d^2 + a_3 d^3$, $d = x - x_0$, cubic pieces joined smoothly, flat beyond the end knots | elevation, distance to river, NCB years, vehicle age |
| **Log size** | $\beta \log(\text{sum insured})$ | contents sum insured |

When a spline input is **missing**, the curve is switched off and a separate coefficient is used:
$f_j = \beta_j^{\text{miss}}$. It is a level of its own, not an average.

```{ojs}
md`The sum-insured term is an **elasticity**: β = ${logSI.toFixed(3)}, so doubling the sum insured multiplies
contents cost by 2<sup>${logSI.toFixed(3)}</sup> = ${Math.pow(2, logSI).toFixed(2)}, a rise of ${Math.round((Math.pow(2, logSI) - 1) * 100)}%, not 100%.
Bigger homes don't claim proportionally more.`
```

### Large claims: GLM plus a Pareto tail

Above the threshold $u = 50{,}000$, claims are too few and too wild for a GLM alone. The large-claim GLM sets the
*shape* (who is likely to have one), and a **generalised Pareto distribution (GPD)** fitted to the excesses sets
the *level*:

$$
P(X - u > y \mid X > u) = \left(1 + \frac{\xi\,y}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[X - u \mid X > u] = \frac{\sigma}{1 - \xi}\quad(\xi < 1)
$$

The Pareto adjustment $A$ rescales the GLM so the large-claim cost matches the fitted tail rather than the few
observed claims:

$$
A \;=\; \frac{\sigma / (1 - \xi)}{\overline{(x - u)}_{\,x > u}}, \qquad
\mu^{\text{large}}_i = A \cdot \exp\!\big(\eta^{\text{large}}_i\big)
$$

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(tail.map(d => ({
  line: d.line, "large claims": d.n_large, "shape ξ": d.shape, "scale σ": d.scale,
  "fitted mean excess σ/(1-ξ)": d.mean_excess_fitted, "observed mean excess": d.mean_excess_empirical, "adjustment A": d.adjustment
})), {format: {"shape ξ": x => x.toFixed(3), "scale σ": x => Math.round(x).toLocaleString(), "fitted mean excess σ/(1-ξ)": x => Math.round(x).toLocaleString(),
  "observed mean excess": x => Math.round(x).toLocaleString(), "adjustment A": x => x.toFixed(4)}})
```

For motor, the observed excesses include the single 11.89m bodily-injury claim. On its own it adds about 20,000 to
the observed mean excess over 591 claims (11.84m / 591). The fitted Pareto mean is lower, and $A = 0.765$ scales the
GLM down to match the fitted tail rather than that one claim.

### From model to prediction

$$
\hat P_i \;=\; \big(\mu^{\text{small}}_i + \mu^{\text{large}}_i\big) \times s_{\text{segment}}
$$

```{ojs}
md`The level step *s* moves each segment halfway (geometrically) from the developed-market level towards the emerging
market's own 2023-24 experience: contents ×${model.lines.contents.segments.ren[0].value.toFixed(4)}, motor renewals
×${model.lines.motor.segments.ren[0].value.toFixed(4)}. Motor new business is set to ×1.05 of the as-is cost, because
new business claims more and is 77% of the 2025 book.`
```

### How it is scored: Tweedie deviance and $D^2$

The competition (and every backtest on this site) scores with the Tweedie unit deviance at $p = 1.5$:

$$
d(y, \mu) = 2\left(\frac{y^{2-p}}{(1-p)(2-p)} - \frac{y\,\mu^{1-p}}{1-p} + \frac{\mu^{2-p}}{2-p}\right),
\qquad
D^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_i d(y_i, \hat\mu_i)}{\sum_i d(y_i, \bar y)}
$$

$D^2$ is the share of deviance explained relative to predicting the average for everyone: 0 means no better than
the average, and 1 is perfect. With so many zero-claim policies, values of 0.08-0.16 are good.


```{ojs}
exTerms = model.lines[exLine].components[exComp].terms
```

```{ojs}
exInputs = model.lines[exLine].inputs
```

```{ojs}
viewof exTerm = Inputs.select(exTerms.map(t => t.term), {label: "Factor", format: t => {
  const term = exTerms.find(x => x.term === t); return term.kind === "log_si" ? "Sum insured" : (exInputs[term.input]?.label ?? t)
}})
```

```{ojs}
exT = exTerms.find(t => t.term === exTerm)
```

```{ojs}
levelLabel = (input, v) => {
  const o = exInputs[input]?.options?.find(o => o.value === v); const l = o ? o.label : v
  return l === "true" ? "Yes" : l === "false" ? "No" : l
}
```

```{ojs}
{
  const t = exT
  if (t.kind === "categorical" || t.kind === "band") {
    const rows = t.kind === "categorical"
      ? (exInputs[t.input]?.options ?? Object.keys(t.levels).map(v => ({value: v}))).map(o => ({level: levelLabel(t.input, o.value), rel: Math.exp(t.levels[o.value] ?? 0), base: o.value === t.base}))
      : [...t.bands.map(b => ({level: `${b.lower ?? "-∞"} < x ≤ ${b.upper ?? "∞"}`, rel: Math.exp(b.contribution), base: b.contribution === 0})),
         ...(t.missing ? [{level: "missing", rel: Math.exp(t.missing), base: false}] : [])]
    return Plot.plot({
      width: 860, height: Math.max(200, 34 * rows.length + 60), marginLeft: 170,
      x: {label: "Relativity (1 = base level)", grid: true, type: "log", tickFormat: "~f"},
      y: {label: null, domain: rows.map(d => d.level)},
      marks: [
        Plot.ruleX([1], {stroke: "#64748b"}),
        Plot.barX(rows, {y: "level", x1: 1, x2: "rel", fill: d => d.rel >= 1 ? "#e15759" : "#16a34a", fillOpacity: 0.8, inset: 4}),
        Plot.text(rows, {y: "level", x: "rel", text: d => `×${d.rel.toFixed(3)}${d.base ? " (base)" : ""}`, dx: 6, textAnchor: "start"})
      ]
    })
  }
  const inp = exInputs[t.input]
  const lo = t.kind === "log_si" ? 5000 : t.grid_min, hi = t.kind === "log_si" ? 150000 : t.grid_max
  const step = Math.max(inp?.step ?? 1, (hi - lo) / 300)
  const ref = t.kind === "log_si" ? 30000 : null
  const f = x => t.kind === "log_si" ? Math.exp(t.coefficient * (Math.log(x) - Math.log(ref))) : Math.exp(splineValue(t, x))
  const pts = d3.range(lo, hi + step / 2, step).map(x => ({x, y: f(x)}))
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 860, height: 340, marginLeft: 60,
    x: {label: t.kind === "log_si" ? "Sum insured (relativity 1 at 30,000)" : inp.label, grid: true},
    y: {label: "Relativity", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(pts, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#1d4ed8", strokeWidth: 3, tip: true}),
      t.kind === "spline" && inp.allow_missing ? Plot.ruleY([Math.exp(t.missing)], {stroke: "#e15759", strokeDasharray: "5 4"}) : null,
      t.kind === "spline" && inp.allow_missing ? Plot.text(["unknown"], {x: hi, y: Math.exp(t.missing), dy: -7, textAnchor: "end", fill: "#e15759"}) : null
    ]
  })
}
```

the same engine as the calculator.


```{ojs}
exRes = scorePolicy(model, "contents", {...exCase.policy, exposure: 1})
```

```{ojs}
exComp0 = exRes.components.small
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table([
  {step: "Intercept (base)", value: "", "log contribution": exComp0.intercept, relativity: Math.exp(exComp0.intercept)},
  ...exComp0.terms.map(t => ({step: t.kind === "log_si" ? "Sum insured" : (model.lines.contents.inputs[t.input]?.label ?? t.term), value: levelLabel2(t), "log contribution": t.contribution, relativity: t.relativity})),
  {step: "Trend to 2025", value: "", "log contribution": Math.log(exComp0.trend_multiplier), relativity: exComp0.trend_multiplier},
  {step: "log exposure (1 year)", value: "", "log contribution": 0, relativity: 1}
], {format: {"log contribution": x => x.toFixed(4), relativity: x => x.toFixed(4)}, rows: 30})
```

```{ojs}
levelLabel2 = t => {
  const inp = model.lines.contents.inputs[t.input]
  const o = inp?.options?.find(o => o.value === t.level); const l = o ? o.label : t.level
  return l === "true" ? "Yes" : l === "false" ? "No" : l
}
```

```{ojs}
tex.block`\eta = ${exComp0.eta.toFixed(4)}, \quad \mu = e^{\eta} = ${exComp0.cost.toFixed(2)}, \quad \hat P = ${exComp0.cost.toFixed(2)} \times ${exRes.steps[0].value.toFixed(4)} = \mathbf{${exRes.final.toFixed(2)}}`
```

## 6. Does it work? Validation

Gerard's rule for every modelling choice: **fit on 2021-23, score on 2024**, developed to ultimate, and keep a change
only if it helps out of time. The chart shows the 2024 $D^2$ of the chosen model against variants that each switch
one piece off.

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 900, height: 420, marginLeft: 230,
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["buildings", "contents", "motor"], range: ["#4e79a7", "#f28e2b", "#59a14f"]},
  x: {label: "2024 out-of-time D² (higher is better)", grid: true, domain: [0.07, 0.12]},
  y: {label: null, domain: backtest.map(d => `${d.line}: ${d.variant}`)},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(backtest, {y: d => `${d.line}: ${d.variant}`, x: "d2_vs_developed", fill: "line", r: d => d.variant === "chosen" ? 8 : 5, tip: true,
      stroke: d => d.variant === "chosen" ? "#111" : null}),
    Plot.ruleX(backtest.filter(d => d.variant === "chosen"), {x: "d2_vs_developed", stroke: "line", strokeDasharray: "3 3", strokeOpacity: 0.6})
  ]
})
```

* **Trend matters for the level:** without it, 2024 predictions fall 5-13% short (predicted / actual 0.87-0.95).
* **The large-claim split helps** buildings and motor.
* **A neural correction (CANN)** was tested on every line and not adopted: the gain wasn't significant over two years.

| Leaderboard | Public $D^2$ |
|---|---|
| Part 1 (developed market), Gerard's final candidate | **0.12805** |
| Part 2 (emerging market), C0 with the level steps | **0.15805** |

Alan's separate comparison in `workings/home_insurance_model` found the same: explainable Tweedie GLMs beat XGBoost on
the 2024 holdout on every line, so nothing was lost by choosing a model the board can read.

## 7. Governance

* **No leakage:** customer service contacts, renewal decision and written premium are never used.
* **Portable factors only:** region, occupation, credit band, exact ages, mileage and telematics are dropped, because
  the emerging market doesn't have them (D-31).
* **Explainable by design:** every prediction decomposes into the table above. The calculator shows it for any policy.
* **Reproducible:** the calculator's engine is tested against an independent Python scorer on every build
  (4,010 policies, worst difference about 4 in 10^15).

*Sources: Gerard's `export/excel` (terms, splines, scalars), `docs/MODEL_DOCUMENTATION.md` and `audit/evidence`;
Alan's `workings/home_insurance_model`.*
